textPreview: A Cooja-based study of evolving RPL attacks, whole-seed adaptation, Sybil identity manipulation and local explanation

text: Supervisors: Dr Swagato Sanyal and Dr Prosanta Gope
textPreview: Supervisors: Dr Swagato Sanyal and Dr Prosanta Gope

text:
Good morning. My name is Al-Mizaan Jamal. This dissertation asks a simple but important question: what happens when an intrusion detector learns one attack pattern and the attacker later behaves differently? I investigate that question using RPL, the routing protocol used by constrained Internet of Things networks. I built and validated attack scenarios in Contiki-NG and Cooja, converted their behaviour into a controlled dataset, tested static transfer and supervised adaptation, added a Sybil identity attack, and finally used a local language model to explain the measured evidence. The title remains focused on explanation under concept drift. The Cooja work is the controlled cybersecurity environment that makes that explanation problem measurable.

text:
The easiest way to understand concept drift is to think about pattern matching. A detector learns from the past. In the green box, it sees Blackhole behaviour, where packets disappear after an attacker starts dropping forwarded traffic. In the red box, the malicious behaviour changes. A Sinkhole may continue forwarding but advertise an attractive rank, while a Sybil node pretends to be several identities. The old detector can then miss the attack because the evidence no longer looks like the pattern it learned. In this dissertation I create that change deliberately by training on one attack family and testing on another. This is a controlled concept-drift scenario, not proof that all real-world drift behaves the same way. The next slide explains why the LLM-focused project required this controlled experimental environment.

text:
The project began with the question of whether a language model could explain anomaly detection under concept drift. Before an LLM can explain anything reliably, it needs real structured evidence. That created the need for a controlled cybersecurity experiment. I therefore used Contiki-NG and Cooja to generate repeatable routing attacks, known activation times and matched controls. The IDS then converts those observations into predictions, recall, F1, feature shifts and drift alerts. Only after that does the language model receive the structured evidence and produce a readable explanation. Point to the three statements at the bottom. The detector makes the classification. The experimental pipeline produces the evidence. The LLM explains that evidence. It does not inspect Cooja by itself and it does not replace the IDS. Next I will show the paper that shaped the adaptive-detection idea.

text:
This is the main paper that shaped the dissertation. The figure on the left shows changing malicious activities arranged as attack profiles over time. That is the idea I adapted. I did not reproduce the complete NetSim adversarial reinforcement-learning system or copy its Algorithms 1 and 2. Instead, I mapped the research question into a smaller and more auditable Cooja experiment. Multiple RPL attack families replace the paper's changing profiles. Contiki logs and routing state replace the NetSim observation stream. Whole-seed adaptation tests recovery after the attack mechanism changes. I also implemented standard DDM and DQN or DDQN principles in narrower extensions, with my own Cooja-derived states, actions, reward design and evaluation protocol. SVELTE separately motivated the importance of protocol-aware routing evidence. The honest claim is a Cooja-based extension of the underlying drift and adaptation question. Next I will explain the RPL mechanisms being changed.

text: DODAG = a routing graph toward the root
textPreview: DODAG = a routing graph toward the root

text:
RPL is the IPv6 routing protocol used by constrained low-power networks. It organises nodes into a Destination-Oriented Directed Acyclic Graph, or DODAG, leading toward a root. The easiest way to think about rank is that it describes a node's relative position in that graph. Nodes exchange DIO control messages to advertise routing information, and DIS messages to request it. The attack families in this project change different parts of that process. Blackhole and Grayhole affect forwarding. Sinkhole and Increase Rank manipulate route attraction. DIS Flood and DIO Suppression change control traffic. Worst Parent changes parent choice. Wormhole changes the apparent path. Sybil changes identity. Point to the four callouts. This diversity is exactly why one feature representation may work for one attack and fail on another. The next slide shows how all of those mechanisms enter the experimental system.

This is the map of the whole dissertation. On the left, Cooja executes the Contiki-NG applications and modified RPL behaviour. Each completed attack has a matched control and five seeds. The simulator produces logs, radio traces and routing events. Those are converted into sixty-second windows while preserving which complete run and seed each row came from. The middle stage tests static cross-attack transfer, whole-seed adaptation and online change detection. The final stage packages the measured evidence for a local Qwen model running through Ollama. The nine labels at the bottom are the completed campaign, not a proposed list. The key separation is shown in the final sentence. Detection, drift monitoring and explanation are distinct tasks. The next slide explains the timing and leakage control that make the evaluation defensible.

text:
Every baseline scenario runs for five hundred and forty simulated seconds. The attack begins at two hundred and forty seconds, after the network has had time to form routes. I then extract sixty-second feature windows. The important methodological point is the split shown at the bottom. Each simulation produces several related rows. A random row split could place some windows from seed 123456 in training and other windows from the same run in testing. That would let the model benefit from run-specific behaviour and make the score optimistic. I therefore keep each complete seed on one side of the split. During adaptation, the model receives one or more complete target-attack seeds and is evaluated on different unseen seeds. Point to the green correct split. That whole-seed rule is central to the credibility of the results shown later. Before training any model, however, I first verified that the attacks themselves were executing.

text:
Before making any machine-learning claim, I checked that each attack activated and produced the intended protocol-level effect. The left side shows the real Cooja environment with sixteen motes and the log listener. On the right are preserved lines from completed runs. The Blackhole hook begins dropping forwarded packets after four minutes. The Sinkhole advertises rank 128 while preserving its internal rank of 256. The Sybil node rotates the source identity used for outgoing DIO messages, here showing fd00::f001. These markers validate the implementation and establish ground truth, but they are not included as predictive features. Across nine families there are forty-five attack and forty-five matched control runs. This step matters because a labelled dataset is only meaningful if the label corresponds to behaviour that actually occurred. The next slide shows how these raw events become the IDS dataset.

text:
This slide follows one sixty-second observation from raw evidence to model input. Cooja produces packet and routing events. The extractor groups those events into fixed windows and computes traffic, control-message, rank, parent and identity measurements. A label describes whether that window belongs to normal operation or the post-activation attack period. The family, seed, mode and attack markers remain in the dataset for provenance and validation, but they are not predictors. The frozen dataset contains eight hundred and ten windows from ninety complete run groups. It has eighty-four columns, of which fifty-seven are generic predictive features. Sixteen attack-marker or provenance fields are explicitly excluded from the model. This design makes it possible to audit exactly where a row came from without allowing the classifier to read the answer. With that foundation in place, the next slide presents the central static-transfer result.

text:
This heatmap is the central concept-drift result. Each row is the attack family used for training, and each column is a different family used for testing. The colour represents held-out F1, which balances precision and recall. Recall tells us how many attack windows were actually detected. Forty-eight of the seventy-two off-diagonal CART combinations have zero attack recall, meaning the detector missed every attack window in those changed environments. Only six pairs reach F1 of at least zero point eight. The mean cross-attack F1 is zero point one eight two. Accuracy alone would hide part of this failure because control and pre-attack windows are labelled normal. The correct conclusion is that static cross-attack transfer is brittle under this controlled distribution shift. It is not a claim that CART can never work, and it is not proof about every form of field drift. The next slide explains why feature representation changed one of the most important conclusions.

text:
This slide shows the most important methodological correction in the project. The early Blackhole-to-Sinkhole experiment used coarse traffic and radio features. Static F1 was zero, and even after three Sinkhole seeds the F1 was only zero point zero nine eight. The reason is mechanical: Blackhole changes forwarding, while Sinkhole changes advertised rank and route attraction. Retraining cannot recover information that the feature set never records. I therefore added persistent low-rank, parent and routing-state evidence. With those features, one complete Sinkhole seed raises held-out F1 to zero point eight one three, and three seeds raise it to zero point nine seven three with recall zero point nine five and no false positives in this campaign. Point from the red side to the green side. The lesson is not that retraining always works. Adaptation works when the representation exposes the new mechanism. The next slide asks how much target data is needed across all nine families.

text:
Whole-seed adaptation asks how much labelled evidence from the changed environment is required. At zero target seeds, the model only knows the source attack and mean F1 is zero point one eight two two. Adding one complete target seed produces the largest recovery, increasing mean F1 to zero point eight two five eight. Two seeds reach zero point eight six six four, and three reach zero point eight seven nine two. The evaluation always uses different complete target seeds, so this is not training and testing on windows from the same simulation. The curve supports rapid average recovery, but it does not mean every source-target pair improves monotonically. Some pairs remain unstable or fail completely, especially when the features still do not distinguish the changed mechanism. I would therefore describe this as strong average supervised recovery with important pair-specific limitations. The next slide focuses on Sybil, the identity-based extension that creates a deliberately different attack surface.

text:
A Sybil attack means one real node pretends to be several different identities. Before activation, node sixteen uses one normal source identity. After activation, it rotates virtual IPv6 identities in outgoing RPL DIO messages. This attack was selected because it changes the evidence surface. A forwarding or rank detector can appear healthy while identity consistency has changed. Static models trained on other families transfer poorly to Sybil, with mean target F1 zero point two one eight. After one complete Sybil adaptation seed, held-out F1 rises to zero point nine six eight. I also implemented a transparent identity monitor. It alerts on all fifty post-activation attack windows and on none of the forty-five control windows in this controlled address plan. That monitor is not a universal deployed Sybil defence. It is a mechanism-specific observable that demonstrates why identity evidence matters. The contribution is the implementation and evaluation within this Cooja drift framework, not the invention of Sybil attacks. The next slide separates online change detection from adaptation.

text: CUSUM reacts earlier because the monitored rank-state feature changes before delayed labels arrive.

text:
CUSUM and DDM answer a different question from adaptation: when should the system suspect that something has changed? CUSUM, or cumulative sum control, watches a measurement over time and alerts when the change becomes consistently too large to look normal. Here it watches the low-rank routing-state signal. DDM, or Drift Detection Method, watches the classifier's mistakes, so it depends on delayed labels and reacts later. Across five Sinkhole attacks and five controls, both detectors alert on all attacks and no controls. CUSUM alerts in the first post-activation window, while DDM alerts one sixty-second window later. The sample is small and controlled, so the zero control-alert rate is not a field false-alarm estimate. The result shows that mechanism-aware telemetry can provide an earlier trigger than waiting for the classifier's labelled error rate to deteriorate. Next I test whether the main adaptation result survives changed radio conditions and compare its direction with the supplied external data.

The robustness campaign adds sixty simulations with attacker relocation and a lossy radio model. After three target seeds, adapted F1 remains near one across Blackhole, Sinkhole and Sybil. The weakest condition is lossy-radio Sybil at F1 zero point nine three seven, with false-positive rate zero point zero four six. This supports robustness within the evaluated simulator conditions, not physical deployment generalisation. I also analysed the supplied Gope dataset separately. A Gaussian model trained on Blackhole and tested on Sinkhole achieves recall zero point zero four seven and F1 zero point zero eight eight, showing the same direction of weak cross-attack transfer. Those values must not be ranked directly against Cooja because the simulator, schema, labels and split units differ. Together, the results support the transfer problem while keeping the validity boundary explicit. The next slide reports three more complex extensions, including negative results.

text: Extra complexity is useful only when it improves the correct objective without unacceptable network cost.
textPreview: Extra complexity is useful only when it improves the correct objective without unacceptable network cost.

text:
These extensions produced important negative results. First, the trust layer turned routing observations into interpretable forwarding, rank, control and route signals, but it did not change CART F1. It is therefore presented as diagnostic evidence, not a performance improvement. Second, the active Sinkhole defence rejected suspicious routes too aggressively. Application responses fell by about seventy-nine percent, radio transmissions increased by over five hundred percent, and the network switched parent hundreds of times. Detection confidence alone is not enough for safe routing intervention. Third, the isolated DQN and DDQN controllers selected update actions on recorded Cooja-derived streams. DDQN improved over DQN, but neither beat the simple always-incremental baseline. This is not the full live adversarial system from Gope et al. These results strengthen the dissertation because they show where intuitive extensions fail and why operational cost matters. The next slide returns to the local language-model explanation layer.

text:
The local explanation layer runs Qwen two point five, three billion parameters, through Ollama on the same computer. It does not receive thousands of raw Cooja lines. It receives a structured evidence package containing feature changes, IDS results, drift alerts, adaptation outcomes and limitations. The example here is based on the real Sinkhole case. The model identifies the increase in low-rank observations and the lower non-root rank, describes possible drift, assigns medium confidence and asks for further investigation. I ran all nine attack cases locally. The outputs were schema-valid, produced no unsupported-claim flags under the project's rule-based screening, and achieved a mean score of seven point seven eight out of ten. That score is an automatic evidence-alignment screen, not a human analyst study and not proof of factual correctness. Some outputs use imprecise terminology, which remains a limitation. Point to the bottom sentence: the IDS detects; the LLM explains. The next slide shows the concise live demonstration plan.

text:
This slide summarises how the research improved through failure analysis. The first Sinkhole adaptation attempt failed because the representation was too coarse, so I added routing-state evidence. I identified that random window splitting could leak related rows, so all evaluations preserve complete seeds. Trust features did not improve predictive F1, so I narrowed the claim to diagnostic interpretation. The active defence caused major network disruption, so I report it as a failed prototype and derive requirements for hysteresis, confidence and route stability. The DQN and DDQN controllers did not beat always-incremental updating, so I keep the simpler baseline as the stronger result. These are not side notes. They show that the project changed its method and its claims in response to evidence. That critical correction process is part of the dissertation contribution. The final slide now states only what the completed evidence supports.

text:
The evidence supports five conclusions. First, static cross-attack transfer is brittle: forty-eight of seventy-two CART pairs miss every attack window. Second, feature representation determines whether adaptation is even possible. Third, adding one complete target seed gives the largest average recovery, although some pairs remain unstable. Fourth, Sybil provides a distinct identity-based surface and becomes strongly detectable after limited supervised adaptation or through a transparent identity-specific monitor. Fifth, the local language model can turn structured evidence into a readable explanation, but it is not the detector and its automatic score is not a human usefulness study. The project is simulation-based and does not claim physical deployment performance or a full reproduction of Gope et al.'s adversarial RL architecture. The central conclusion is shown at the bottom: changing attacks require both adaptive detection and understandable evidence. Thank you. I welcome your questions.
